description: Solo team building "Earth Jukebox" for the challenge "The Earth Information Jukebox": a web app that turns NASA Earth Information Center visualizations into live music. Pick a visualization like a record, press play, and the app analyzes each video frame in real time (color, brightness, motion) and translates it into a musical soundscape. Built with accessibility in mind: keyboard control, screen reader support and spoken descriptions for blind and low-vision users.
summary: NASA's Earth Information Center shows our changing planet in pictures, and those pictures store their data as colour. If you cannot see the colours, the data is out of reach. Earth Jukebox reads the colours back into what they stand for and tells you in sound and in words. Point at any spot of a visualization and you hear a tone and get a label such as "Warm water, about 26 °C, Indian Ocean". Press Play and the parts of the picture, such as north, tropics and south, take turns as notes while each one is named. It runs as a web app with eight NASA visualizations and as a browser extension for NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio pages. Every sound is generated live from the frame on screen, so blind and low-vision users can explore Earth science on their own.
details:
Earth Jukebox lets you select a NASA Earth Information Center visualization and experience it together with a soundscape that is generated in real time from its visual frames. It adds one thing the challenge really needs: the sound is explained. A sonification only helps a blind or low-vision listener if they can tell what a sound means.

Point: move the mouse over the picture, or use the arrow keys, and a tone follows the data under the pointer. Higher means warmer, thicker or more. A label next to the pointer gives the value and, on flat world maps, the name of the sea or region with coordinates. Hold still and a voice reads it out.

Play: the picture is split into a few parts, for example north, tropics and south. They sound one after another, always in the same order, and the part that sounds is outlined and labelled. Lightning is played as ticks like a Geiger counter, so you can hear storms shift between the hemispheres with the seasons.

Learn the sounds: every record has buttons that play each sound on its own, and a Describe button that speaks what the visualization shows, what its colours mean and what the current values are.

How it works: about ten times a second the current video frame is drawn onto a small analysis canvas. Each record has a decoder that turns a pixel colour back into a data value or "no data", using the visualization's own colour scale: the rainbow temperature scale of the ocean currents map, the four particle colours of the aerosol map, the yellow flash dots of the lightning globe. The decoded values drive a synthesizer built with the Web Audio API and the labels on screen. Nothing is pre-recorded.

Browser extension: the same code is packaged as a Chrome extension that adds a "hear this picture" button to pages of NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio and lays the point-and-listen layer over the picture or video there.

Accessibility: full keyboard control, spoken output through the browser's speech synthesis, a live region for screen readers, visible focus and high contrast. You can also open your own picture or video.

Limits: values are estimated from colour, so they are approximate and not the original model output. Place names are coarse. Two of the eight records, carbon dioxide and night lights, only read brightness.

Built with plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, the Web Audio API and the Web Speech API. No frameworks or external libraries. ffmpeg was used to scale down the NASA videos and to assemble the demo video. Code, texts and demo video were made with AI assistance (Claude); the demo voice-over is synthetic speech.
